title: Anthony Fauci's Darkest Hours
snippet: Anthony Fauci's Darkest Hours
hay:
anthony fauci's darkest hours anthony fauci's darkest hours

authored by jeffrey a. tucker via the brownstone institute,

“out, damned spot! out, i say!” said lady macbeth as she paced in a hallucinatory state, reliving in her subconscious the murders she helped plan. she rubbed her hands as if washing them, to wash away the sin, following up the promise to her son that “a little water clears us of this deed.”

the line comes to mind from the latest dump of entries from the diaries of anthony fauci that cover the months december 2021 to may 2022. these were the darkest months of the covid era.

confidence that the virus was a lab creation was growing. that points directly to fauci. the lockdowns had given rise to growing population-wide fury. and the shot was not working, not stopping infection or spread while groups reporting deep injury from injection could not be censored fast enough to make them vanish completely, though tech companies certainly tried.

fauci still held his position at niaid with certainty that he would keep it under president biden, whose confidence he enjoyed. he was daily in touch with the people who were actually running the government – aides ron klain and jeff zients – and coordinated his decisions with them. they trusted him to continue the covid operation, which they all knew to be a national security issue beyond the control of any political player. fauci was the front man but an effective one, until he became a liability.

we know from previous entries that fauci at first hoped the new virus would get lost in the mix of a bad flu season. this was mid-january 2020. the cdc called him out on that. his first scheme failed because a savvy businessman in china spilled the beans by posting the sequence on a pay-to-play website in mid-january.

after pressing a friend and former colleague to use his personal credit card to download the sequence, fauci launched plan b, which was to deny the lab leak and prepare a nationwide inoculation to make it all go away.

the audacious scheme was to keep population immunity at the lowest levels possible through lockdowns while the shot went through clinical trials and was ready for distribution. fauci knew for certain that this was the type of virus that would mutate rapidly. his hope was to take the energy out of the pace of mutation by reducing the infection rate as low as possible.

sadly for him, the new and most powerful variant had appeared just as his shots hit general distribution. delta disabled their protection that had been formulated for wild type and alpha. the race was on, as mutations appeared faster than repeated boosters could catch.

the spot would not go away no matter what he did.

the darkest hours open with the appearance of omicron in december of 2021, the fastest spreading but least virulent strain. he now had a new problem. with omicron operating as a form of inoculation itself, there was less reason for vaccination than ever, especially given the risk of injury. and yet his goal of 90 percent coverage was nowhere in view, while population opposition to the entire covidian regime was rising.

fauci might as well have thrown up his hands, admitted defeat, apologized for putting the country through the biggest trauma of our lifetimes, and ruining the lives of students everywhere, in addition to crushing the dreams of millions of small business owners.

but that is not who he is. he would not and could not accept responsibility for doing this. he ended up demonizing the opposition, scrambling for cover, wrapping himself in ever more layers of fame for protection, and clinging to the lies he told himself as self-justification as his career and legacy were permanently tarnished beyond repair, even as he developed a severe and strange case of germaphobia in a macbeth-like way.

two weeks before this tranche begins, biden had gone on tv to declare the following: “we are looking at a winter of severe illness and death for the unvaccinated – for themselves, their families and the hospitals they’ll soon overwhelm. but there’s good news: if you’re vaccinated and you have your booster shot, you’re protected from severe illness and death.”

it was an intense claim even as the weakest of all variants had just appeared, even as evidence poured in that these injections provided no protection whatsoever. regardless, the biden administration was dedicated to ruining a second holiday season with terrifying warnings all in the hope of maximum shot coverage.

fauci begins his diary close to christmas in a dispute with the cdc, which was starting to open up a bit and lighten up on its diktats. it wanted to permit people to choose whether to get tested yet again after recovering from covid. fauci smelled a rat – that dread thing called freedom – and tried to strangle the baby in the crib.

meanwhile the opposition campaign gained new steam from the release of robert f. kennedy, jr.’s masterpiece, the real anthony fauci, and he had headlined a rally on capitol hill that galvanized a movement. fauci was aware of the growing opposition but was mostly dismissive.

by february 2022, pressure was rising to open up the economy and society and fauci was on the backfoot. he was still defending china-style lockdowns before he later claimed never to support them at all.

fauci began collecting international endorsements to assure himself of the good job he had done.

the white house, meanwhile, was increasingly concerned about the sheer number of military men and women who had quit rather than submit to vaccination. what kind of militia might they form if it came to that? fauci claimed not to be worried about that at all, observing that they must not have liked their jobs very much. this is a man entering into deep denial.

meanwhile, he was being more honest with himself about the lack of efficacy of the shots themselves.

his fame and stardom became his only solace, the warm blanket in which he wrapped himself for comfort from the storms outside.

another strange feature of this period is how fauci became absolutely obsessed with avoiding any possibility of catching covid. he started panicking in crowds, taking his own advice ever more seriously. he started cancelling dinners and meetings.

thinking through why, consider that he knew that this virus was created in a lab and he knew that the shots would not protect against it. he now had fully two years to turn over these facts in his brain. they began to eat at him more and more. no matter how many times he boosted himself, his paranoia only grew worse.

by the spring, even fauci started admitting that both he and the cdc were completely making things up. there was no science to anything they were saying and he knew it. even he had lost faith in the system he created, playing a scientist only on tv.

by late april, fauci was starting to clamor for other ways to understand all that had unfolded. maybe the great barrington declaration had been correct all along? he could never admit it to himself. but his egregious failures to control the virus through any means finally led him there through a side door.

that said, fauci’s own personal germaphobia only intensified to the point that it was debilitating.

this tranche ends with fauci’s paranoias growing, his fears of the opposition intensifying, and finally mollifying his psychological breakdown by reflecting on his own global fame, which he regarded as his only real hope to avoid the consequences of all that he had done.

fauci was finally pushed out of his job later in the year, mostly because of growing concerns that the more he talked, the more the resistance to vaccination grew. there are even indications in this drop that it was industry itself that pushed him out for doing such a bad job in selling their product. he found safe haven at georgetown university in a high-paid post.

and where are we today? fauci will talk with no one, no reporters, not even on background. his last public appearance consisted of 110 invocations of his right to remain silent under the 5th amendment.

the spot never went away, no matter how much sanitizer he rubbed on his hands. “life’s but a walking shadow, a poor player,” he might be saying to himself, “that struts and frets his hour upon the stage, and then is heard no more. it is a tale, told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing.”

us designates helium a critical material in reindustrialization push to avoid "single point of failure" us designates helium a critical material in reindustrialization push to avoid "single point of failure"

america's reindustrialization depends on securing reliable, conflict-free supplies of critical materials, including rare earths and other critical metals, most of which are produced and processed overseas.

the trump administration has made rebuilding and strengthening domestic critical material supply chains a national security priority. its designation of helium as a critical material on friday morning extends that effort to now include the industrial gas used for semiconductor manufacturing and many other applications.

the energy department's decision earlier today makes the 20th critical material designated by the agency and brings the industrial gas within the energy act of 2020's critical materials framework, including closer government monitoring.

energy secretary chris wright wrote in a statement, "president trump is bringing back america's manufacturing industry, and that means making sure we have the materials needed to build things in america again."

wright continued, "helium is essential to producing the semiconductors and advanced technologies that power our economy. by designating helium as a critical material, we are taking another step toward securing our supply chains, creating american jobs, and ensuring the united states leads the world in energy and technological innovation."

helium is recovered as a byproduct of natural gas processing and faces growing geopolitical risks in the gulf area. qatar's exports have been severely curtailed by iran's closure of the strait of hormuz and attacks on qatari infrastructure, while russia imposed temporary export controls in april.

the good news is that the us remains one of the top helium producers in the world, supplying 81 million cubic meters in 2025, or about 43% of global output. it exported 38 million cubic meters that year.

helium is critical to applications ranging from chipmaking to medical imaging to quantum computing to magnets to space rockets.

assistant energy secretary audrey robertson warned that shortages could become a "single point of failure" for strategically important industries. the canadian press quoted her in an interview.

"we need to make sure that we can build those here. and helium is one of those components that could be a single point of failure, where we cannot let that happen. that's why we're designating it within our statutory authority, but i think why it's important is not necessarily for our birthday parties," robertson said in an interview. "it's really towards the future of american competitiveness and energy security, which we believe is national security."

designating helium as a critical material under the energy act of 2020 brings it within doe's framework for developing, demonstrating, and commercializing critical material technologies to support america's reindustrialization efforts.

the new designation could help qualifying helium projects access government financing, technical assistance, and partnerships, similar to support provided to rare earth miners.

title: DOJ Seeks Appeals Court Intervention In California Ballot Lawsuit
snippet: <span property="schema:name" class="field field--name-title field--type-string field--label-hidden">DOJ Seeks Appeals Court Intervention In California Ballot La
hay:
doj seeks appeals court intervention in california ballot lawsuit doj seeks appeals court intervention in california ballot lawsuit

authored by aldgra fredly via the epoch times,

the department of justice (doj) filed a notice of appeal on oct. 22 in its bid to block california from counting mail-in ballots from voters whom the federal government suspected of being noncitizens.

the doj asked the ninth circuit court of appeals to intervene after u.s. district judge david carter failed to rule on its emergency application for injunctive relief by noon thursday, the deadline set by the department.

the department said the judge's silence amounted to what it called a "constructive denial" of its emergency application for preliminary injunctive relief, citing the "critical and exigent nature" of the case.

the doj sued california on oct. 15 to prevent the counting of mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 people identified by the federal government as likely noncitizens.

the federal government asked that if california was not able to independently confirm the citizenship of the voters registered, the state should set aside ballots received until citizenship could be confirmed.

los angeles county said on oct. 15 that it could not comply with the doj's demand because the department has not provided evidence, sources, or methodology to establish that the individuals identified in its records were ineligible to vote.

"we cannot withhold or refuse to count ballots based solely on unverified allegations, nor can we disregard the legal requirements governing our election - and we certainly have no authority to act on records that are outside of our jurisdiction," the county said in an oct. 15 statement.

in its oct. 21 emergency filing for a temporary restraining order, the doj said state and county officials contended they lacked the mechanisms and authority to prevent noncitizens from voting in the midterm elections.

the department argued that this showed an immediate threat to the integrity of lawful votes.

"as defendants continue processing ballots that cannot later be segregated or verified for eligibility, the dilution of lawful votes accelerates in real time," the doj said in its filing.

"this is an emergency. every minute of processing that occurs without segregating the ballots of suspected non-eligible voters causes untraceable disenfranchisement and dilution of the votes of united states citizens."

los angeles county filed a motion on oct. 21 asking the judge to dismiss the doj's lawsuit, arguing the department lacked legal standing to bring the case.

"the executive, like any other plaintiff, must identify a concrete injury, actual or imminent, fairly traceable to the county's conduct and likely to be redressed by the requested relief. the complaint identifies none," it said.

acting u.s. deputy attorney general trent mccotter sent a letter to the los angeles county counsel's office on oct. 16, saying the doj did not expect county officials to adjudicate anyone's immigration status, but asked the county to temporarily set aside ballots when there are credible concerns about the voters' eligibility.

mccotter warned that county officials could risk "becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime" if they knowingly count ballots from individuals whom federal agencies have identified as noncitizens.

in response to the letter, los angeles county registrar-recorder dean logan said his office is focused on conducting a fair and secure election.

title: "We Should Not Have Done It": Thiel Breaks With Trump Over Iran War, Warns America May Not "Have The Hard Power"
snippet: <span property="schema:name" class="field field--name-title field--type-string field--label-hidden">"We Should Not Have Done It": Thiel Breaks With Trump Over I
hay:
"we should not have done it": thiel breaks with trump over iran war, warns america may not "have the hard power" "we should not have done it": thiel breaks with trump over iran war, warns america may not "have the hard power"

one day after we reported that donald trump jr. has privately broken with his father over the iran war, peter thiel, the paypal and palantir (pltr) co-founder who was the first big tech investor to back trump in 2016 and the biggest funder of super pacs behind jd vance's 2022 senate run, has also drawn a line in the sand over trump's defining foreign-policy gamble.

in audio from an oct. 12 private lecture in nashville obtained by decoded by politico (calder mchugh), thiel told the room:

"i'm skeptical of [the war], i think we should not have done it. there were a lot of mistakes that were made."

"maybe we don't have the hard power. maybe we're going to lose the soft power war."

in other words, one of the architects of the maga-tech alliance now thinks the war was a mistake and that america may not be strong enough to finish it. the scoop crossed overnight:

🚨🇺🇸🇮🇷 peter thiel, one of trump's most influential billionaire backers, says the iran war was a mistake

"i think we should not have done it. there were a lot of mistakes that were made."

thiel made the comments last week during a private lecture in nashville.

he also raised... pic.twitter.com/fktnpb91sm

— mario nawfal (@marionawfal) october 22, 2026

thiel on the iran war: "i think we should not have done it" https://t.co/0jg5vucy0r

— alex burns (@alexanderburns) october 22, 2026

below we walk through what thiel said, the even stranger parts of the lecture, and why it lands at exactly the wrong moment for the white house.

"the sword of damocles"

per politico, thiel spent much of the lecture on what he called the unchecked power of the international criminal court, drawing on rumsfeld and cheney, and then said this:

"i read the cheney family's trump derangement syndrome as an attempt to buy favor with the [international criminal court] and avoid prosecution. probably too late... and i have come to suspect that the threat of an icc arrest warrant is the sword of damocles hanging over the trump administration as it tries to persecute this war in iran."

("persecute" is the word in politico's transcript. we assume he meant "prosecute," though at this point in the war, who knows.) translation: the president's most cerebral backer is publicly speculating that trump officials face war-crimes exposure. very reassuring.

thiel also recounted a meeting with benjamin netanyahu in early 2024, after oct. 7, in which he asked about israel's plans for gaza. according to thiel, netanyahu replied: "i can't just dresdenize it," a reference to the allied firebombing that killed roughly 25,000 people.

still on team trump (sort of)

to be fair, thiel didn't defect. politico says he "highlighted his continued support of trump and suggested he wanted to protect the president," and framed his critique as opposition to neoconservatives and middle east wars rather than to trump personally. that's the vance-wing argument, and politico reported back in march that vance himself was "skeptical" of striking iran before the war began. neither thiel's representatives nor the white house responded to politico. put differently, this is the restrainer wing of the coalition saying in private what it can't say from the podium, and the audio got out 12 days before the nov. 3 midterms.

* * *

title: Why Are Scientists Suddenly So Concerned About An Asteroid Hitting Earth?
snippet: <span property="schema:name" class="field field--name-title field--type-string field--label-hidden">Why Are Scientists Suddenly So Concerned About An Asteroid H
hay:
why are scientists suddenly so concerned about an asteroid hitting earth? why are scientists suddenly so concerned about an asteroid hitting earth?

authored by michael snyder via end of the american dream,

authorities assure us that we are perfectly safe and that no giant space rocks are heading our way. if that is true, why is a scenario that has been developed for the 2027 planetary defense conference "based around a hypothetical impact threat" from a very large asteroid? and why are scientists at lawrence livermore national laboratory studying how to destroy a giant asteroid that is heading toward earth using nuclear weapons? if there is no threat anywhere on the horizon, wouldn't you think that those scientists would have something better to do with their time? on top of everything else, nasa recently concluded a secretive operation known as "osiris-rex" in which a spacecraft visited an asteroid, plucked a piece off of it, and returned it to earth. while the general public is being told that we are safe for decades to come, a tremendous amount of time, money and energy is being poured into preparing for a potential asteroid threat.

do they know something that the rest of us do not?

i am convinced that there is far more going on behind the scenes than we are being told.

they never say anything that will alarm the general public, but at the same time they are pumping vast resources into "sophisticated planetary defense efforts" that are intended to protect our planet "from potentially hazardous asteroids"...

would we be prepared if a potentially life-threatening object from space were on a collision course with earth? and how much damage could an incoming asteroid actually cause?

such questions remain at the forefront of increasingly sophisticated planetary defense efforts aimed at protecting our planet from potentially hazardous asteroids. yet even if astronomers are able to identify a space object that might pose a threat, a significant number of uncertainties remain: the object's size, composition, structure, and potential impact locations all must be considered, as these factors can dramatically influence what happens once an asteroid enters earth's atmosphere.

if there are no near-earth objects that are a threat, why spend so much money on this?

we certainly have a lot of other very pressing matters that do require funding right now.

nasa is either wasting our money, or something else is going on.

interestingly, nasa is a participant in the 2027 planetary defense conference. an exercise is underway that simulates how authorities would respond to a "tunguska-sized object" that is headed toward earth...

additionally, nasa's center for near-earth object studies (cneos) regularly participates in planetary defense exercises designed to test these assessment methods, with current scenarios under development for the 2027 planetary defense conference that take a cue from one of history's most concerning airburst events.

"the current exercise that is underway for the 2027 planetary defense conference is based around a hypothetical impact threat from a roughly tunguska-sized object," wheeler told the debrief.

for those of you that are not familiar, in 1908 the tunguska event flattened approximately 2,000 square kilometers in siberia...

tunguska event, enormous explosion that is estimated to have occurred at 7:14 am plus or minus one minute on june 30, 1908, at an altitude of 5-10 km (15,000-30,000 feet), flattening some 2,000 square km (500,000 acres) and charring more than 100 square km of pine forest near the podkamennaya tunguska river in central siberia (60°55′ n 101°57′ e), russia. the energy of the explosion is estimated to have been equivalent to the explosive force of as much as 15 megatons of tnt - a thousand times more powerful than the atomic bomb dropped on hiroshima, japan, on august 6, 1945.

why hold an exercise of this nature if there is absolutely no threat of this sort of event occurring for decades to come?

and why did nasa just send a small spacecraft to grab a piece of an asteroid known as bennu and bring it back to earth?...

on sept. 30, nasa formally concluded osiris-rex, the historic first u.s. mission to pluck a pristine piece of an asteroid and deliver it safely back to earth.

the van-sized osiris-rex spacecraft - whose name is short for origins, spectral interpretation, resource identification, security-regolith explorer - visited and sampled bennu, an ancient space rock holding pristine remnants from the dawn of our solar system more than 4.5 billion years ago. among those cosmic relics are raw organic building blocks, the kind that may have seeded life on earth.

"i have known this day was coming for a long time, but it is still difficult to see it arrive," osiris-rex principal investigator dante lauretta, who's based at the university of arizona, said in a post on linkedin. "i feel enormous pride in what we accomplished together, and real sadness that this journey has come to an end."

that was certainly an impressive scientific achievement.

but it also cost a lot of money to do that.

why not spend all that money in more productive ways if asteroids are no threat to us?

and why study how to destroy asteroids using nuclear weapons if there won't be any asteroids to destroy for the rest of this century?

a shocking study that was recently conducted by scientists at lawrence livermore national laboratory is raising a lot of eyebrows...

a new study from lawrence livermore national laboratory (llnl) has used advanced 3d simulations to assess how effective a nuclear weapon would be for destroying a dangerous space object such as a large asteroid on a collision course with earth.

yeah, that definitely sounds a lot like a bruce willis movie that i once watched.

but in that case, a civilization-killing space rock was actually headed toward us.

why are our scientists running so many simulations if we are facing absolutely no threat?...

for their new work, the team ran simulations to explore how an asteroid might be affected by a nuclear blast somewhere near its surface, with the aim of rapidly heating and vaporizing material within it.

they began with more than 1,500 one-dimensional simulations to test the approach before running three fully three-dimensional simulations modelling the effects of a nuclear blast on a roughly 160-meter (525-foot) asteroid, altering factors such as the distance to the asteroid when detonation occurred and assumptions about how easily it would be damaged by such an explosion.

"these simulations give us a much more detailed picture of how an asteroid may respond to a nuclear mitigation attempt," isaiah santistevan, who led the study, said in a statement. "being able to model damage, fracture and material motion in three dimensions is an important step toward improving our ability to evaluate planetary defense options."

more resources are being devoted to "planetary defense" than ever before in our history.

is this being done for a reason, or is this just a colossal misallocation of public funds?

those of you that have been following my work for an extended period of time already know what i think.

i believe that there are very serious threats out there that are not being discussed publicly.

it is always policy to keep the general public as calm as possible when we are facing a very serious threat.

that means not telling the general public the truth.

of course everyone should be able to see that our particular neighborhood of the cosmos has been unusually busy lately.

i asked google about this, and this is the response that i got...

yes, data from the american meteor society and usa today confirms an unusual and significant surge in large fireball events during the first quarter of 2026, especially through march

this week, we are witnessing the peak of the orionid meteor shower...

the orionid meteor shower reaches its peak tonight, wednesday, oct. 21, and continues into early thursday morning. the shower is made up of debris left behind by halley's comet, which burns up as it enters earth's atmosphere.

under dark, ideal conditions, the orionids can produce about 10 to 20 meteors per hour. but a bright waxing gibbous moon will hide some of the fainter streaks. nasa says the moon is expected to set around 3 a.m. local time, giving skywatchers a darker window before sunrise.

the fireballs in the sky that people are marveling at right now are no threat.

but there are giant space rocks that are looming in the distance.

one of these days, our luck will run out and one of them will hit us.

when that day arrives, everything will change and millions will suddenly die.

title: Selling Gas Twice: Venture Global Courts Qatar While Plotting A $160 Billion AI Power Empire
snippet: <span property="schema:name" class="field field--name-title field--type-string field--label-hidden">Selling Gas Twice: Venture Global Courts Qatar While Plottin
hay:
selling gas twice: venture global courts qatar while plotting a $160 billion ai power empire selling gas twice: venture global courts qatar while plotting a $160 billion ai power empire

seven months ago, qatar was the world's biggest lng seller. now it's a buyer.

according to a reuters scoop late thursday, qatarenergy is in advanced talks with venture global (vg) on a long-term supply deal for at least 3 million tons of lng a year, sourced from vg's cp2 plant, which is still under construction in louisiana. the report landed just hours after qatarenergy signed a separate deal with cheniere (lng) for up to 4 million tons a year through 2054. vg shares jumped more than 6% on friday, and they have now roughly doubled this year. then again, they're still trading about 45% below their $25 ipo price.

venture global's other headline this month is that it wants to get into ai data centers... in a very big way. goldman thinks both stories come back to the same molecule. below we summarize what goldman's lng team has been telling clients about each (available to pro subs), and why we think the qatar trade is the one that pays first.

the customer who used to be the competition

regular readers know how qatar got here. in march, iranian missiles hit ras laffan, the world's largest lng complex. we wrote at the time that the attack itself was "bad" and the math behind the global lng fleet "far worse", and a day later we concluded that qatar had been dethroned as "lng king", with the us taking the crown. the strikes damaged two of qatar's 14 trains, taking out 12.8 million tons a year, or about 17% of export capacity. qatarenergy ceo saad al-kaabi said repairs would take three to five years and cost roughly $20 billion a year in lost revenue.

the bill has been coming due. last week we reported that qatar's government revenue plunged 42% in the first half: lng exports were just 1.6 million tons in september, less than a quarter of the prewar average, and kpler sees october falling to 0.6 million tons. qatarenergy has also been renewing its force majeure notices every month, most recently through november.

meanwhile, doha still has customers to serve. so it has been buying spot cargoes, many of them from venture global, and is now trying to lock in long-term supply. as one source told reuters back in september, "they will have to buy whatever they can get their hands on." we flagged where this was headed the moment bloomberg first reported the talks:

qatar buying lng?

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) september 10, 2026

goldman's americas pipelines & mlps analyst john mackay ran the numbers that same day in "outlining contractable capacity for our lng coverage following media reports of qatarenergy interest". mackay notes that qatar is "the largest single lng exporter in the world," sits behind the strait of hormuz, and "is planning the largest lng capacity additions through the medium-term." goldman says it takes no view on whether a deal happens, but it points out who would be on the other side if one does:

we note that venture global (vg, buy) management stated during our mid-august virtual ndr that such deals could be a sign of significantly tighter global lng balances than the market currently expects. to illustrate the scale of available capacity, we outline below the uncontracted capacity within our coverage universe, which totals ~69 mtpa potentially available by ye32. specifically, we project up to 40 mtpa / 9 mtpa / 7 mtpa / 12 mtpa of contractable capacity at vg / lng / next / glng, respectively... in our view, vg and golar lng (glng, buy, on cl) are well-positioned due to their ability to offer meaningful capacity with flexibility around timing.

put differently, vg alone has about three times as much uncontracted capacity as qatar lost at ras laffan. rapidan's count of capacity under construction is more modest, but vg still leads it at 10 mtpa, ahead of cheniere and woodside (6 mtpa each) and sempra's port arthur (3 mtpa). so when qatar goes shopping in the us, venture global probably can't be avoided.

mackay brought qatar up again in his 3q26 preview on oct 8. he trimmed his 3q ebitda estimate to $2.52 billion, below the $2.61 billion consensus, but kept fy26 at $9.03 billion, "still at the top-end of guidance." he also wrote that "any qatar contracting, on top of their ongoing spot deals, would be meaningful." that was two weeks before the reuters scoop. goldman also counts recent additions such as conocophillips' 20-year deal (oct 1) and china gas as "high-quality," while dismissing the adverse galp arbitration ruling on cp1, where damages are capped at $170 million, as "manageable." goldman's price target stays at $18, about 32% above friday's price.

two caveats. nothing has been signed yet: reuters "could not immediately learn the timeline of any agreement... or how long a contract could run," and neither company commented. and cheniere's deal doesn't start until 2031, which says a lot about how long doha expects to be without those trains.

plan b: burn it for ai

the qatar news is relatively straightforward. the data center plan is a far bigger swing.

on oct 15, vg signed frame agreements with ge vernova (gev) and baker hughes (bkr) for up to 16 combined-cycle "power island" units of 720 mw each, plus transformers and switchgear. vg says the units could support up to 10 gw of compute by the end of 2034. the plants would run behind the meter, without drawing on the grid or local water utilities, around vg's existing louisiana lng sites. vg plans to place its first power island order by year-end and was set to file its first permit applications that week. it already runs 4.5 gw of gas-fired generation in island mode to power its lng plants.

goldman's first take, called it "on its face, a major diversification away from vg's core lng export focus," but listed five ways it could fit with the lng business. the fifth is the most interesting:

...an admittedly amorphous but potentially meaningful ability, over time, to "switch" between liquefying gas for export and burning it for compute.

in other words, vg would own an option on which use pays more for a molecule of louisiana gas: a qatari utility or a hyperscaler. that's the "sell gas twice" pitch.

the market wasn't convinced. vg was up 1.5% in the premarket, according to goldman's industrials & natural resources desk, which called it a "big diversification for vg." the stock then closed down 5.8%. investors seem to be asking the same thing as mackay: whether vg can fund the rest of its lng buildout to ~85-100 mtpa before taking on a second capital-intensive business. goldman also notes that "strip pricing would add ~$20b to our ebitda estimates, all else equal, by ye30." that's a good reminder that the lng business is the one generating the cash.

"a relatively low-cost call option"

goldman hosted ceo mike sabel and cfo jack thayer for a virtual roadshow the next day. the oct 19 takeaways note, "significant potential power scope, but limited spend ahead of customer deals" is where the numbers got big:

...their plans are potentially massive, specifically >10 gw by 2034 and ~$160b of deployed capital, with typical scope effectively being a powered shell solution (~teens million of capex per mw) vs. smaller-scale behind-the-meter (btm) solutions (generally ~$1-2m/mw)... potential scope aside, vg's current commitments are relatively small - specifically ~2 power plant commitments and a few hundred million dollars in capex, with firm off-ramps before meaningful capital is spent, and could be redeployed for their lng expansions and/or resold if commercial wins do not materialize.

some math: $160 billion for 10 gw works out to about $16 million per mw, roughly ten times the cost of a typical behind-the-meter project, because vg would supply the land and buildings as well as the power (everything except the chips). about two-thirds of that capex isn't power-related, and vg says it won't commit to that part without signed tenants. for the power portion, management is targeting ~75% investment-grade debt financing. if the power piece is the remaining third, or about $53 billion, that's somewhere around $40 billion of new debt on top of a balance sheet that already carries a debt-to-equity ratio of about 3.5x.

goldman, which rates vg buy, ends up more constructive than the tape:

overall, we expect the broader power trade could remain choppy in the near-term and believe investors will look for more confidence in commercial execution before giving more credit to vg (as we have recently seen for others in the data center power market, including wmb, kgs, and lb in our coverage). that said, we come away from the conversation increasingly viewing the strategic rationale of the bkr/gev agreement as effectively a relatively low-cost call option for vg, with a mostly limited impact on the story if the broader power macro story doesn't re-inflect - and with significant potential upside over time if it does.

wells fargo, which had been sitting at equal weight, apparently agrees: it upgraded vg to overweight on tuesday and raised its target from $15 to $21. the "choppy" part is easy to see: as goldman's desk showed a couple of weeks ago, ipps and ge vernova were trading near their "liberation day" lows on a p/e basis.

cheap power, slow power

we've been pounding the table on on-site generation for almost a year. since last november, we have argued that every data center should have its own "behind the meter" power so that households don't pay for the ai buildout through their electric bills. a month later we put it more simply:

make "behind the meter" mandatory https://t.co/bcbnwx2e5g

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) december 24, 2025

wall street has since come around. goldman now expects behind-the-meter generation to power a quarter of all us data centers by 2030. so vg's idea is sound. the problem is timing, and it comes down to which technology vg picked. combined-cycle gas turbines (ccgts) are the cheapest behind-the-meter option and also the slowest. bernstein's machinery team spelled out that trade-off last month in "powering ai: the modular advantage" (also available to pro subs): ccgt power costs about $48/mwh, but it takes 4-5 years to deliver, versus months for fuel cells at almost twice the price.

that lines up with goldman's timeline: first deployments in late 2028 at the earliest, and only about half of the capacity ramped by 2031. by then, vg will be competing for tenants with everyone who signed up two years earlier. goldman flags this too, asking about "their go-to-market strategy for signing customers as a relatively later entrant vs. other competitors in the space."

equipment is the other constraint. back in september we noted that the gas turbine shortage was sending ai developers back to boilers and steam. vg's ge vernova and baker hughes order secures a big block of a very scarce resource, and as goldman notes, vg is already one of those suppliers' largest customers. there's a twist here, too. as bloomberg's stephen stapczynski pointed out in march, qatar's two damaged trains need new gas turbines for their refrigeration compressors, with delivery expected to take 2-4 years. so the same turbine backlog that keeps qatar's capacity offline is the one vg has just reserved a large chunk of.

one molecule, two bidders

vg now has two possible new markets for its gas. one is a state-backed buyer that has lost a sixth of its capacity for years and needs cargoes now. the other is a data center business that doesn't yet have a single tenant and can't deliver power before 2028. goldman's view is that the power plan is a cheap option and the lng business keeps generating the cash in the meantime:

...the size of their agreement and their track record of disruption in lng should argue for vg upside over time as well as a potentially meaningful shift in competition for the btm power and epc sectors.

we agree with the first half. the qatar deal is close to signing, the counterparty is about as motivated as a buyer can be, and every month ras laffan stays damaged makes 20-year american lng look more valuable. the $160 billion data center plan is a different matter: until vg names a tenant, it is mostly equipment reservations and press releases. to its credit, vg knows this, which is why it built in "firm off-ramps." the bigger risk may be the timing. if hormuz reopens properly and qatar's trains come back sooner than expected, the spot cargoes, and maybe the urgency to sign long-term deals, could fade just as the power build starts requiring real money.

for now, the market is rewarding the qatar story and punishing the ai one: shares jumped over 6% on a reuters report of talks and fell 5.8% on 10 gw of compute. we'll know more on nov 10, when vg reports third-quarter results.

much more in the full goldman notes (here, here and here) all available to pro subs.

title: Trump Says He Will 'Veto Everything' If Democrats Win Midterms
snippet: <span property="schema:name" class="field field--name-title field--type-string field--label-hidden">Trump Says He Will 'Veto Everything' If Democrats Win Midter
hay:
trump says he will 'veto everything' if democrats win midterms trump says he will 'veto everything' if democrats win midterms

authored by jack phillips via the epoch times,

president donald trump told reporters on friday that he plans to use his veto power on bills or resolutions democrats want to pass if they win in either the house or the senate, with days to go before the november midterm elections.

"i think the republicans are going to win - but if there was gridlock, what happens is i veto everything, and then the democrats come and want to make a deal," he said.

when pressed further on congressional gridlock if democrats win congress, he responded by saying that historically, a president would then "veto, veto, veto, and they come and they say, 'how do we get it done.' and we make a deal."

trump has issued two vetoes during his second administration, while his predecessor, former president joe biden, used his veto power 13 times. in his first term, trump vetoed 10 measures.

in recent weeks, trump has held campaign-style rallies in numerous states to boost republican voter turnout ahead of the nov. 3 election.

on thursday, the president traveled to iowa to support ashley hinson, iowa's republican nominee for the u.s. senate, for a rally in sioux city. the visit to safe territory is geared toward boosting gop turnout as trump is expected to visit the state again on nov. 1.

"let's go out and do what we do best, which is to win," trump said in the rally, thanking iowans for their support.

throughout the campaign cycle, trump has often said he would back certain provisions, including sending payments to americans, if republicans retain control of the house of representatives and the senate. the gop currently holds small majorities in each chamber.

last month, trump said at a dallas rally that he would send $5,000 payments to americans in what he called a dividend derived from tariff revenues and investment into the united states.

he also sent out $500 health insurance rebate checks, which he said are meant to offset costs incurred under the biden administration, as well as a $90 one-time payment to people receiving medicare.

trump also announced at a kansas rally to back sen. roger marshall's (r-kan.) reelection bid that he would back a measure to support the year-round availability of e-15 gasoline, which is blended with a higher amount of ethanol than regular gasoline, but said he would only back the provision if marshal wins his reelection bid next month.

according to the university of florida's election lab, as of friday, more than 22 million people have voted early in the midterms, including more than 10 million early in-person voters and more than 12 million mail-in ballots returned. overall, more than 59 million mail ballots have been requested.

only new hampshire, missouri, alabama, and new york have not reported any data to the election lab, according to a map the school provided.

as for trump, he told reporters on friday as he was going to depart for fort myers, florida, that he might be "voting tomorrow."

saturday marks the first day of early voting in florida, and it runs through oct. 31. at another point in the gaggle with journalists, trump was asked about this year's early voting figures and which party has benefited.

"nobody knows," he responded.

title: Space War Fears Rise As Russian Satellite Makes Dangerous Maneuver
snippet: <span property="schema:name" class="field field--name-title field--type-string field--label-hidden">Space War Fears Rise As Russian Satellite Makes Dangerous Ma
hay:
space war fears rise as russian satellite makes dangerous maneuver space war fears rise as russian satellite makes dangerous maneuver

authored by rfe/rl staff via oilprice.com,

us officials publicly accused russia of threatening a finnish-operated commercial satellite that provides imagery and intelligence to ukraine and other nations, calling the move "deliberately reckless."

in response to the accusations, made during a united nations debate on october 21, russia broadly described us claims as "absurd" and accused washington of its own "aggressive military space ambitions."

the back-and-forth came days after a russian military satellite known as kosmos-2612 moved "dangerously" near to iceye-x36, a satellite registered in the united states and operated by a finnish company called iceye.

the russian satellite came "exceptionally close" - within 200 meters, by some estimates - something that space officials and amateur satellite watchers said was extremely unusual.

"this was not a routine conjunction or 'fly by,'" leolabs, an aerospace intelligence company, told rfe/rl. "the behavior is consistent with sophisticated rendezvous and proximity operations."

iceye-x36 carries a radar technology that can gather detailed terrestrial images, even through cloud cover. the finnish company in january signed a contract with the ukrainian defense ministry to provide intelligence.

kosmos-2612 "exhibited threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite," brian hardesty, an adviser to the us delegation to the conference on disarmament, said during a meeting in new york of the un first committee, a body that debates arms control and disarmament issues. "these behaviors appear consistent with an on-orbit weapons operation."

"the decision to conduct these activities was deliberately reckless," he said.

russia's representative who could not be immediately identified, did not directly address the assertion.

"we call on member states to give the proper response to the aggressive military space ambitions of the united states," he said.

he also referenced comments made last month by the secretary of the us air force, the top civilian official for that military branch.

as just announced in the @un first committee, russia's cosmos 2612 military satellite has been exhibiting threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite, behaviors consistent with on-orbit weapons operations. this violates long-established safety thresholds in low earth orbit. the united states will continue to secure and defend american vital national security interests in, from, and to space.

— under secretary of state thomas g. dinanno (@undersect) october 21, 2026

speaking to a conference outside of washington, troy meink's comments that washington has in fact deployed actual weapons in space - "on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action" - caused a jolt among policy experts.

other longtime space watchers, however, said the announcement merely stated publicly what had already been obvious for some time.

"the united states did not suddenly weaponize space by acknowledging that it possesses these capabilities," wrote mallory stewart, a former top arms control secretary at the us state department. "an arms race in space has been under way for years."

title: Nikola Founder Trevor Milton Accuses FBI Agent Of Witness Intimidation As New Report Challenges His Claims
snippet: <span property="schema:name" class="field field--name-title field--type-string field--label-hidden">Nikola Founder Trevor Milton Accuses FBI Agent Of Witness In
hay:
nikola founder trevor milton accuses fbi agent of witness intimidation as new report challenges his claims nikola founder trevor milton accuses fbi agent of witness intimidation as new report challenges his claims

trevor milton, founder and former ceo of electric truck maker nikola and now ceo of jet company syberjet, is suing an fbi agent and a whistleblower who testified against him during his fraud trial, alleging they conspired to intimidate a potential defense witness ahead of his trial.

milton filed a complaint on october 13 in federal court in utah against fbi special agent christopher s. essick and nikola whistleblower paul lackey. the lawsuit alleges essick secretly controlled two anonymous x accounts, @cntrlscrut1nizr and @lfxs1212, which posted negative commentary about milton and nikola, discussed betting against the company's stock and allegedly harassed former nikola executive jason roycht.

milton claims the online activity contributed to roycht's decision not to meet with his defense attorneys before his trial.

but before an answer was filed in his latest lawsuit, a new investigation by activ8insights has raised questions about key allegations in milton's latest lawsuit, including his claim that an fbi agent operated anonymous social media accounts used to target him and a potential witness.

in what appears to be a detailed investigation, activ8insights reported that it identified and interviewed the person operating both twitter accounts, finding evidence that appeared to contradict milton's allegations. the account holder purportedly showed reporters his government-issued photo id, vehicle registration and insurance documents, all bearing a name other than essick's. he also demonstrated control of both x accounts by sending messages from each during a live video call.

the individual denied knowing essick or having any connection to the fbi and said no one else had ever controlled the accounts.

milton defended his lawsuit in an interview with activ8, saying his investigators had gathered evidence connecting essick to the accounts. he suggested the agent may have transferred control to another person or directed others to post on his behalf.

"he could have traded them off. he could have handed them off," milton said. “look, it’ll all come out in the lawsuit… we’re going to come in with depositions. we’re going to come in with discovery."

the report questioned milton's decision to bring the lawsuit in utah. the complaint cites interactions with an x account called @life_utah as part of its argument that the alleged conduct was directed at the state. however, the account's operator told activ8 he does not live in utah.

according to the complaint, none of the parties named in the lawsuit resides in utah, raising questions about whether the federal court has jurisdiction.

the lawsuit comes after milton suffered a separate legal defeat in his case against cnbc and short seller hindenburg research, which published a damaging report about nikola in 2020. in december 2025, a new jersey appeals court ruled against milton in a lawsuit stemming from a 2022 episode of cnbc's american greed that examined nikola and the fraud allegations surrounding the company.

milton had accused cnbc of trade libel and hindenburg of helping spread damaging allegations. the appeals court concluded that his claims concerned alleged harm to his personal reputation rather than his business and were barred by the one-year statute of limitations for defamation.

the court ordered the lawsuit dismissed with prejudice and a new jersey judge ordered the nikola founder to reimburse cnbc $286,087 in attorneys' fees and litigation expenses. hindenburg research was also ordered to be reimbursed by milton to the tune of $270,475 in fees.

milton was indicted in 2021 on securities fraud and wire fraud charges and convicted in 2022 of defrauding investors and later sentenced to four years in prison, though president donald trump pardoned him in march 2025.

milton has continued to challenge the circumstances surrounding his prosecution, arguing that he was unfairly targeted. he has moved on to become ceo of syberjet, a company focused "on cutting-edge aerospace technology" that includes, among other things, developing ai assisted flying.

title: Appeals Court Allows Mississippi Ban On DEI, Removes Judge Over AI Use
snippet: <span property="schema:name" class="field field--name-title field--type-string field--label-hidden">Appeals Court Allows Mississippi Ban On DEI, Removes Judge O
hay:
appeals court allows mississippi ban on dei, removes judge over ai use appeals court allows mississippi ban on dei, removes judge over ai use

authored by zachary stieber via the epoch times,

mississippi can enforce a law prohibiting some diversity practices in schools, a federal appeals court ruled on oct. 22 in a decision that also removed the judge overseeing the case over the use of artificial intelligence.

the u.s. court of appeals for the fifth circuit ruling overturned a 2025 decision from u.s. district judge henry wingate that blocked the state from enforcing a law restricting diversity, equity, and inclusion (dei) practices.

the law, h.b. 1193, bars schools and colleges from promoting dei through classes and administrators from punishing students for their views on dei.

wingate said the law violated the constitutional rights of teachers and students, siding with plaintiffs such as the jackson federation of teachers.

the fifth circuit disagreed.

circuit judges said the orders blocking the law fell short because they cited only two cases to conclude the law violates first amendment rights and brushed off a framework outlined by the supreme court in a decision known as moody for future first amendment cases.

"the district court brushes off the moody framework as a 'supposed' formality that was satisfied merely because plaintiffs identified programs and books that, in their view, are 'arguably on the chopping block,'" circuit judge jeffrey smith wrote for the unanimous fifth circuit panel.

"that does not come close to satisfying the inquiry demanded by moody. it is egregious for the district court just to assume that plaintiffs' assertions that certain materials are 'on the chopping block' must mean a constitutional violation has occurred, without any independent legal analysis whatsoever."

under the framework, a plaintiff must show a law's unconstitutional applications "substantially outweigh" constitutional applications. the two-step process includes establishing the scope of the law and then comparing what would and would not be constitutional.

"the district court's remaining substantive reasoning is poor at best," smith said. "judge wingate cites a couple of parents who were allegedly worried about the law's impact; the fact that defendants are 'loudly noncommittal,' something bordering on paradoxical that has nothing to do with legal analysis; and, on vagueness, the passing thought that 'if [h.b. 1193] lives down to the fears it has generated, has a mouthful of sharp teeth which could inflict deep bites.'"

the mississippi attorney general's office and the teacher's union did not return requests for comment by publication time.

the fifth circuit vacated the preliminary injunction that wingate had entered. it also remanded the case to the u.s. district court for the district of mississippi, but emphasized that a different judge must handle the case going forward.

it cited that wingate's original temporary restraining order included multiple purported facts with no basis in reality, including references to plaintiffs and defendants not named in the complaint and false quotations claimed to be from the law.

wingate later replaced the order without explanation, but the updated order also cited a legal ruling that does not exist.

"the district court - or perhaps, being charitable, its ai agent - ignored and manipulated governing law, apparently to satisfy a policy agenda," smith said.

"because of the extraordinarily grave errors by the district court, we vacate and remand for assignment to a different district judge."

wingate, who did not respond to a request for comment, acknowledged in a letter to the administrative office of the u.s. courts that a law clerk used artificial intelligence to help draft the restraining order and that the initial opinion was a draft that had not "gone through the standard review process."

wingate said he had taken steps to ensure the mistake would not happen again.

title: Data Center Alley Goes Dark: Amazon Abandons Data Centers In Loudoun County
snippet: <span property="schema:name" class="field field--name-title field--type-string field--label-hidden">Data Center Alley Goes Dark: Amazon Abandons Data Centers In
hay:
data center alley goes dark: amazon abandons data centers in loudoun county data center alley goes dark: amazon abandons data centers in loudoun county

finishing a data center in america has become a logistical nightmare. now just starting one is turning into a problem too, even in the one county that was supposed to say yes to everything.

back in april, when we reported that "half of us data centers scheduled to start in 2026, will be canceled or delayed," the blame was spread across the usual suspects: power, transformers, permitting and a vague, growing sense that the locals were getting restless. two months later, blackstone sold its stake in three northern virginia data centers amid grassroot outrage, cashing out of a bet it made less than three years earlier, in the heart of what is known, with zero irony, as "data center alley."

and now the restless locals have claimed their biggest scalp yet.

according to the washington post, amazon has scrapped a plan to build data centers on the site of george washington university's former campus in ashburn, northern virginia, after reaching an agreement with local officials amid widespread opposition from residents. under the deal announced tuesday by loudoun county board of supervisors chair phyllis j. randall, amazon will repurpose the majority of the 122-acre campus for mixed-use and residential development, and commit to never building data centers on the land. it will also donate 25 acres to the county for a community arts center and recreational facility, and hand $5 million to the county's housing fund.

"by choosing dialogue over reflexive disagreement, loudoun county and amazon created an opportunity for the county," randall said in a statement. "this agreement provides new places for our loudoun residents to gather, create, and play. and, most importantly to me, we will provide more attainable homes for working families."

some context on just how big a reversal this is: amazon paid gwu $427 million for the campus earlier this year, roughly four times its assessed value, according to supervisor juli briskman, because the zoning made data centers "a reasonable expectation." it filed a site plan in late july for "bridgefield tech center": four two-story data center buildings totaling more than 800,000 square feet. briskman promptly vowed to fight it "every step of the way," and by september randall was meeting with amazon because a "likely disagreement" was emerging over what the land could legally be used for, per bisnow. amazon's take was that it read the site's legal potential differently than the county, but chose a "shared vision" over costly litigation. translation: amazon also agreed not to sue.

so instead of 800,000 square feet of servers, loudoun gets an arts center, an indoor sports facility, housing, and roughly $70 million in land and cash (the 25 acres carry a stated fair market value of about $65 million). the rezoning alone is expected to take about a year, even on a fast-track schedule. amazon, for its part, is left holding a very expensive future apartment complex.

now for the punchline: according to fortune, loudoun's ~233 data center buildings generated about $1.2 billion in property tax revenue in fiscal 2026, roughly 39% of the county's entire budget. amazon alone says it has invested more than $63 billion in the county since 2011. in other words, the county that arguably needs data centers more than any other in america just accepted a check to make sure one never gets built. if "data center alley" is saying no to data centers, well, who exactly is left to say yes?

the timing was impeccable too. one day later, president trump took to truth social to urge data center developers to "pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a 'dividend'" to win local support, adding "make deals, and get them built!" amazon did pay a dividend, and it did make a deal. it just forgot the "get them built" part.

data center alley, unplugged

amazon's u-turn is the latest in a remarkable string of reversals in what was, until recently, the most data-center-friendly real estate on the planet. regular readers will recall that the trouble started in prince william county, next door, where the 2,100-acre "digital gateway" (up to 37 buildings, ~5gw of capacity and roughly $100 billion of planned spending) was hit by a court ruling that voided its rezoning. in april, brookfield-backed compass pulled out after spending "tens of millions" and years chasing approvals. then came blackstone's sale on june 29... and two days later, we flagged the other shoe dropping:

*blackstone’s qts abandons massive data center in virginia

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) july 2, 2026

then, last month, loudoun's board voted 7-1-1 to draft an up-to-12-month pause on new data center applications, which randall insisted was "not a moratorium" (a 12-month pause being "the maximum allowed by virginia law"). the final vote was due this week; instead, on the same day as the amazon deal, it was pushed to november 17. here is how 2026 has gone in data center alley so far:

note that none of this involves a sputtering hyperscaler running out of money: amazon spent $427 million to buy the land and is now spending another $70 million to walk away from what it bought it for. the capital is there. the permission is not.

the 6% problem

the most striking thing here is how fast "community opposition" went from footnote to deal-breaker. as recently as july, when data center dynamics surveyed 88 industry respondents about their biggest delivery constraints over the next 12 months (a survey bernstein highlighted in its modular-builds deep dive [marketdesk link]), "community opposition/political risk" ranked second to last, at just 6%, behind equipment lead times (24%), power and interconnection (23%), permitting (17%) and supply chains (17%).

three months later, that 6% just killed an 800,000-square-foot amazon campus in the friendliest zip code in america. maybe the respondents should get out more: the heatmap/embold poll that tracks americans' views on a data center "being built near where you live" shows the share strongly opposed going from 24% in august 2025 to 61% in august 2026, while total support collapsed from 43% to below 20%.

and the backlash has gone institutional. in september, wells fargo flagged a fourfold jump in active local moratoriums, to 374 by the end of summer from 92 in june, with the average one lasting nearly a year. its utilities analyst shahriar pourreza summed it up: "dcs are unpopular across the political spectrum." just how bipartisan? in ohio, one of the top data center states, both leading candidates for governor are running on restricting the industry:

ohio is one of the top data center states: aws, meta, googl, msft and sb energy are all building here. both leading governor candidates, democrat amy acton and republican vivek ramaswamy, said they want new restrictions on the industry. acton said she supports what she’s calling a “conditional moratorium” on new data center construction. developers must cover 100% of their own utility costs, build exclusively with union labor, operate with full transparency and meet ohio’s existing air and water quality standards ramaswamy also laid out his data center policy, which he calls his "ohioans-first data center pledge." his campaign describes the plan as resting on three “non-negotiable” requirements: nearby residents must receive free electricity from data center developers, new facilities must pay their full property taxes with no abatements, with that revenue used to fund property tax rebates for homeowners, and developers must meet strict air and water quality standards while prioritizing brownfield sites over farmland. “if a project fails to meet any one of these three requirements, it will not be built. period,” ramaswamy’s campaign states.

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) september 23, 2026

morgan stanley's map of the november races that could tighten the screws further (from its "following ai's $1.6 trillion money trail" report shows 50.8gw of capacity, including 10.6gw already under construction, sitting in states where the elections "could lead to more restrictions on data center construction." texas alone accounts for 24gw, and its governor has already ordered a halt to new data centers pending an audit of 250-300 projects. midterms are 11 days away.

to be fair, not everyone thinks the pitchforks matter. last week semianalysis did a project-by-project audit and concluded that of the ~21gw of capacity sitting in moratorium areas, only about 2.3gw (three projects) is likely to be delayed, which the economist's archie hall described as "much more bark than bite."

perhaps. but here is the thing: the amazon campus was never under a moratorium. loudoun's pause hasn't even been enacted. what killed it was a zoning fight, a threat of litigation and a negotiated "dividend," none of which shows up in a moratorium tracker. which is probably why hall himself sees the bigger risk in deterrence: the projects that quietly never get proposed, or get "re-envisioned" into townhouses before anyone counts them.

goldman's outlook is "largely intact"... assuming half of it never shows up

what does goldman make of all this? in its latest power tracker (available to pro subs) goldman's commodity team argues that "despite rising political push back against us data centers," its capacity estimates "show the 2027 growth outlook is largely unchanged, with moderate revisions." the bank raised its year-end 2026 us data center capacity forecast by 5gw to 64gw, while cutting its year-end 2027 forecast by 5gw to 90gw, and still sees us data center power demand growing 38% in both 2026 (+12gw) and 2027 (+17gw).

so far so bullish. but read the fine print under the chart:

our gs data center capacity forecast assumes only 60/50% of currently scheduled additions are realized, which is derived from the historical relationship between scheduled and activated capacity.

in other words, goldman's "largely intact" outlook already assumes that 40% to 50% of what's on the schedule never gets switched on. which, if we recall, is precisely the "half" we wrote about in april (when sightline climate warned that 30-50% of the ~16gw slated for 2026 would be delayed, with only ~5gw actually under construction), and which semianalysis spent an entire june post telling everyone to "stop saying." goldman, it turns out, never stopped saying it; it just put it in a footnote. and note which way the revision went: the near term got pulled forward, while 2027, the year the hyperscalers are spending like there is no tomorrow for, got cut.

goldman also notes that "effective peak spare capacity tightened yoy across nearly every key region" this summer. that matters, because even the projects that do survive the zoning board walk straight into the next wall.

break ground, then wait for the grid

because getting permission is merely step one. step two is getting power, and that is where the timelines go from awkward to absurd. per berkeley lab data compiled by bernstein, the median time from interconnection request to commercial operation in the us has stretched to over five years, more than triple the 1.5 years it took in 2005.

hence the scramble for "speed to power." goldman's carbonomics team (in its report on "behind-the-meter power solutions for data centers," which we covered in detail last month) lays out the mismatch neatly: a data center takes 2-3 years to develop, while a heavy-duty gas turbine takes 5-7 years to show up. ge vernova, recall, is now taking reservations for 2031 delivery.

then there are the transformers, switchgear and generators that topped the bernstein survey: apollo's torsten slok (who took his number from our june report) pegs transformer lead times at up to 26 months in his latest note, while bloomberg reported earlier this year that delivery times for the large units data centers need had stretched to as much as five years. throw in a chronic shortage of electricians (there is a reason why we told readers to learn to be one back in january) and you get a pipeline where every link must arrive on time for any of it to matter.... which will never happen. as one techradar headline put it, "if one piece of your supply chain is delayed then your whole project can't deliver." correct.

add it all up and morgan stanley's verdict is grim. even after counting every "time to power" fix available (spare grid capacity, nuclear, announced turbines and engines, bloom fuel cells), the bank projects that us data center developers face a 32gw power shortfall through 2028, a result of "intensifying challenges with respect to people, power and politics." that is down from the 44gw shortfall ms warned about last november, which says more about how hard everyone is scrambling for turbines and fuel cells than about any improvement in the grid.

and, as a reminder, the "politics" part of that triad just got a lot worse in virginia, a lot worse in ohio, and possibly a lot worse in texas on november 3. which is why we keep saying the only real solution is to make "behind the meter" mandatory: if the community won't give you its grid, bring your own power plant... and then hope the zoning board lets you build that too.

who wins when nothing gets built

so who benefits from a buildout that keeps getting pushed out? torsten slok had a timely answer this week in "winners and losers if the data center buildout is delayed." the winners are owners of operating data centers ("capacity that is already online can raise rents and fill every megawatt"), holders of powered land and grid access, long-lead equipment makers and on-site power producers. the losers: hyperscalers whose "revenue is capped by supply rather than demand, and committed capex keeps accruing while capacity sits idle," developers and construction-stage investors whose "cash flows start later while interest and carrying costs continue," and equity investors in the ai trade, whose "valuations that assume on-time delivery are exposed to earnings revisions and multiple compression."

slok draws a crucial distinction between delay and cancellation:

a delay hurts returns by pushing cash flows out, but the asset remains and may become more valuable. the real risk is that scarcity unwinds, for example, if supply catches up in a rush or demand softens, which would erode the premium on existing capacity.

which, come to think of it, is a pretty good description of what blackstone did in june: sell fully leased, already operating virginia capacity to digital realty at a scarcity premium, while it lasts. amazon's loudoun campus, meanwhile, falls squarely in the "cancellation" bucket, and joins a fast-growing list. here is the latest update of our ai data center casualty list, which also includes last week's nextdc collapse after protesters stalled power to its melbourne campus:

if loudoun says no, who says yes?

the bulls will say this is one 800,000-square-foot campus in a county that already has 233 data center buildings, and that semianalysis still sees 38gw of us capacity coming online in 2027 (good luck with that). maybe. but the bull case has always rested on the assumption that the binding constraints were physical (chips, power, transformers) and that money could eventually buy its way through all of them. loudoun just showed that money can't buy permission. amazon brought $427 million, a $70 million "dividend" and the threat of a lawsuit, and the best it could get was the right to build townhouses.

despite all this, goldman says the outlook is "largely intact." we'd note that it is intact precisely because goldman already assumes that half of it won't happen, and that the one revision it did make cut 2027. between loudoun's pause vote on november 17, the midterms two weeks before that, and turbine slots booked into the next decade, we suspect that haircut is the floor... and that the next revision (undoubtedly lower) won't be confined to a footnote.

then again, amazon can always try again somewhere else in loudoun... in 12 months, "the maximum allowed by virginia law."

much more in the full goldman power tracker, the morgan stanley "following ai's $1.6 trillion money trail" report and goldman's carbonomics "behind-the-meter power solutions for data centers" note, all available to pro subs.

title: California Man Said ICE Stole His Wife; Police Now Say He Murdered Her...
snippet: <span property="schema:name" class="field field--name-title field--type-string field--label-hidden">California Man Said ICE Stole His Wife; Police Now Say He Mu
hay:
california man said ice stole his wife; police now say he murdered her... california man said ice stole his wife; police now say he murdered her...

authored by catherine salgado via pj media,

a man who accused immigration and customs enforcement (ice) of taking his wife is now in custody under suspicion of murdering her.

there have been some creative excuses to cover up murder, but this might be a first. gurinder gill - immigration status currently undisclosed - first told investigators that his wife went missing after september 30 because ice detained her. detectives subsequently uncovered inconsistencies in his story and dug deeper, coming to the conclusion that she was actually dead, and her husband is the likely guilty party. jasmine and gurinder were in a divorce dispute at the time she went missing.

the biggest tell that his story was bunk, as fox news notes below, is that there had not actually been any ice activity at the gills' home.

a sacramento man allegedly told detectives ice agents arrested his missing wife when she went to get the mail. authorities contacted ice, which confirmed no enforcement activity had occurred at the residence. days before gurinder gill even made that claim, investigators in neighboring el dorado county had already discovered burned and buried remains about 70 miles from the couple's home. those remains were later confirmed to belong to his wife, 30-year-old jasmine gill, an india-born registered nurse and mother of their 8-month-old child. gill, 28, is now charged with murder. the couple had been going through a divorce and child custody dispute when jasmine vanished on sept. 30. her cousin reported her missing on oct. 4. deputies arrested gurinder on oct. 14 and executed search warrants at two homes associated with him. he is ineligible for bail. full story here https://t.co/jm72aa8h5u

— fox news us (@foxusnews) october 20, 2026

as fox also reported, investigators found burned and buried remains, which they have since confirmed as jasmine gill - what gurinder allegedly left of her. apparently, he tried to destroy her corpse about 70 miles from their home. jasmine was born in india, but was a registered nurse in california and the mother of gurinder's 8-month-old baby. part of the couple's struggles was a child custody dispute. as usual, the child will end up suffering most from the craziness of the parent.

jasmine's family started a gofundme to deal with the financial aftermath of her death and help her baby. it describes her as "a daughter, a sister, a nurse, and a mother who deserved so much more." apparently, the family needs money to send jasmine's body back to india, where her mother still lives. fox news did not state whether jasmine is a legal immigrant or not.

sfgate, which obtained the criminal complaint from the sacramento county district attorney's office, also mentioned that gurinder claimed ice arrested his wife while she was getting her mail outside, but that the agency confirmed it had not been to the residence. apparently, gurinder forgot to put out the fire he was using to try to burn his wife's corpse, because authorities discovered her remains after spotting smoke and having to put out a minor forest fire. jasmine's jewelry was also in the burned area.

sfgate also reported:

title: "I Am F**king Getting You!" Unhinged Mayor Lunges At Resident During Chaotic Meeting
snippet: <span property="schema:name" class="field field--name-title field--type-string field--label-hidden">"I Am F**king Getting You!" Unhinged Mayor Lunges At Residen
hay:
"i am f**king getting you!" unhinged mayor lunges at resident during chaotic meeting "i am f**king getting you!" unhinged mayor lunges at resident during chaotic meeting

a new jersey mayor erupted in a profanity-laced tirade during a chaotic public meeting wednesday night, charging toward a resident and threatening him before several people rushed to restrain the furious politician.

pemberton township mayor matthew bianchini, a republican, was caught on camera lunging toward michael sawka, a frequent critic of his policies, as an already contentious council meeting descended into pandemonium.

"i'm fucking getting you," bianchini shouted as others scrambled to prevent a physical confrontation.

the wild incident unfolded while recently fired township official ken gerber, a retired police chief, was addressing council members about his dismissal, which supporters have characterized as politically motivated.

video captured sawka gesturing toward the back of the room before making an obscene gesture toward the mayor. bianchini suddenly sprang from his seat and rushed toward him.

councilman perry doyle jr., a retired police officer, helped restrain the mayor before escorting him away. police subsequently arrived to restore order.

in an interview with wpvi-tv afterward, bianchini conceded to losing control.

"i just basically snapped," the mayor admitted. "i hate to put it this way, but it's a long time coming."

"was it wrong? absolutely. was it justified? absolutely. and i would do it again if i had to," he added.

sawka disputed the mayor's account, insisting he never left his seat, fox news reports.

"i'm just sitting there. i never got up. i sat there the whole time. i was calm the whole time," sawka said.

sawka has filed a municipal court complaint seeking assault and terroristic threats charges against bianchini. police have not announced any charges against the mayor.
